en: The First Canto of the Great Poem *Śrīkṛṣṇavilāsa*, composed by Sukumāra:
There exists the abode of Śrī, the king of mountains named Sumeru, a treasury of all auspiciousness.
Remaining here, he has entered into this entire universe by means of his own self, like Viṣṇu with his mighty [form].
Like two children playing by hiding from one another and looking for each other,
the two moons with their radiant rays quickly circle around its sides, passing the days.
With his high crest and the golden hue of gold, suppressing the darkness with his own radiance,
he shines like a lamp for the three worlds, with the sun moving along its path at its edge.
She, for whose status as a wife the world performs intense austerities out of longing,
is that Earth whom he bears upon his lap like a daughter, she who has the ocean-girdled earth as her sash.

Desiring to dwell upon its peaks, embodied beings perform great acts of charity, sublime sacrifices, and austerities involving the renunciation of food and drink, with minds purified by tranquility. (1.05)
Seated upon the mountain plateaus with their beloveds at the ends of the eons,
the Suras behold the movement of hundreds of waves as the oceans have attained oneness.
There, the flowers of the celestial trees serve as beds, the golden caves are pleasure-houses,
and the sprouts of jewels become lamps for the dalliance of the heavenly nymphs.
Where the inhabitants of heaven, being yellow upon the golden lands, white upon the silver lands,
and blue upon the lands of sapphire, are unable to distinguish one another.
There, the celestial nymphs— trembling at the sounds of the whip-strokes inflicted upon Anūru as he was drawn into the lap of the chariot of the Sun—
immediately embrace him, abandoning the fault of pride toward their lovers.
Because the golden caves within are so bright that the newly-wed brides, unable to look with their faces bowed in modesty,
are led by the Siddhas into the dark caverns of sapphires without any effort at all.
Where, in the groves of wish-fulfilling trees frequented by lovely women,
the feet of Indra’s celestial nymphs— red with lac-dye— shine forth as they rise to gather blossoms.

Even at the onset of the rainy season, the swans in his head-lotus ponds— having bypassed the path of the clouds and never hearing the roar of thunder— do not undertake their long journey to Lake Mānasa.

In the hollows of the Āragvadha trees, from their very roots to their tips, the bees— discerning them by their fragrance— alight upon the branches, which are made beautiful by fresh clusters of blossoms glowing like gold.
The Mandākinī, flowing over its peak and having entered the path of a canal,
acts like a young girl intent on its protection, watering the flower garden day after day.
Delightful in his splendor, the refuge of the gods, and unsurpassable due to his great majesty—
he who shines with a forest garland follows after the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
In ancient times, having assumed the form of the bow of the Lord of Umā with the intent to burn away the three cities,
that bow still bears today the marks of the thunderbolt, the goad, and the fish upon its middle, as well as the impression of his [Śiva’s] fist.
Beholding the stainless faces of the celestial beauties who possess horn-tips, the moon surely travels along their path out of shame, as if to conceal the dark spot upon his own chest.

Once, having approached and offered her salutations, Earth, the abode of lotuses, spoke to him as he sat together with hosts of gods and siddhas upon that mountain peak which is delightful to the mind.
Like a man, I speak something before you; therefore, summon your fortitude. My pain here is merely a pretext, for shamelessness is indeed the cause, and it is the object of universal derision.
The Daityas, created by you and granted boons, now oppress me with their weight;
in both strength and stature, there is no comparison for them, even among the kings of mountains.
Today, as those seeking victory have uprooted rival kings through their own prowess,
the mountains are splitting apart on the battlefields with their mutual lion-roars, terrible as thunderclaps.
When the lord of serpents repeatedly raises his circle of hoods, which have been bent by my weight, with force,
alas, the elephants of the quarters— along with the mountains and oceans shaken by my trembling— cause him distress.
The rays of the sun, obscured everywhere by their constantly wandering armies as they move toward the horizons, do not touch me at all now. (1.23)
"I am exhausted by the burden of the Daityas, and the Lord of Serpents sinks under my weight;
fie upon that plight of the Lord of Tortoises, whose own shell is being shattered by that burden! (1-24)
I am ill at ease upon the lord of serpents, whose circle of hoods is sinking under my weight;
I am on the verge of falling, like a riverbank whose roots have been washed away by the force of the current.
"O King, this has been reported by me; the fault of speaking what was not asked should not be imputed to me.
Suffering is reported by those who are to be protected; beyond that, Your Majesty is the authority. (1.26)
When Pṛthivī had thus spoken appropriately, the Lord, the Master of Creatures, remained motionless for a moment through the power of his meditation;
then, gazing upon the faces of the nectar-eating gods, he spoke as follows.
"It is not untrue what the Earth has said: 'I have obtained the good fruit of my own actions.
For it is because I have prospered that these Daityas, disregarding me, are forcibly oppressing the worlds."
What would be gained by lingering attachment to past actions, which are censured by all who possess complete knowledge?
O gods, strive for their swift uprooting for the welfare of the worlds! (1.29)
Arise at once; enough with anxiety, for anxiety is an obstacle to action.
Let us go wherever Nārāyaṇa—the night of destruction for the Dānavas—may be found upon this earth.
Saying "So be it," the hosts of gods and Siddhas accepted his words with great reverence;
then the Lotus-born One set out through the air with them toward the presence of the Lord of the Universe.

The Creator beheld in no long time the shore of the ocean, which was most excellent with sandalwood trees embraced by cardamom creepers, and whose rows of waves were breaking as they reached the shoreline— exactly as he had desired in his mind.
And he beheld the ocean consisting of milk, its masses of foam raised high like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa,
[stirred] by the plunging of the auspicious Lakṣmī’s companions who were eager for sport in the sacred waters.
The fragrance of the tulasī from the chest of Vaikuṇṭha— exceedingly meritorious, wafted by the wind, and what remained after being inhaled by the circle of sages— delighted those dwellers of heaven.
With eyes directed according to the fragrance, the immortals, led by Hiraṇyagarbha,
beheld the abode of the Kaustubha jewel upon the chest of Murāri, which resembled the newly risen sun.

Having heard the sound of the songs of the celestial nymphs of Vaikuṇṭha— blended with the sky-piercing resonance of musical instruments and having all mental fluctuations concealed— they became filled with joy.
Perceiving their attachment, those gods, assuming humble attire and placing their hands upon their own heads,
gazed upon the Lord of All, who possessed a physical form like the merit of all living beings personified.
Resplendent with abundant golden ornaments, dark as a tamāla tree, and reclining upon the ocean,
he resembled a rain-cloud laden with streaks of lightning, rendered unable to rise because of having drunk too much water.
He gracefully honors with his gaze the conch-shell Pāñcajanya, which is being filled by the wind from the waves of the ocean and held in his left hand as it turns sideways. 1.39.
At every moment, through the honors bestowed by the Lotus-Seated Goddess arising from her special affection,
he wipes away the humiliation of being churned from the ocean that had been previously inflicted upon himself.
Alternately placing a lotus held in her hand upon the path of her eyes, she repeatedly brings about sleep and awakening; I gaze with a smile upon her as she sits in the lotus posture.
It bore the luster of a banyan tree, dense with a mass of shining fruits, by means of the network of the Lord of Serpents' hoods reflected in its own clear body.

He was like a vast, venerable lake that was constantly filled with the sound of its ruddy geese and conchs, exceedingly serene, the abode of lotuses, and the dispeller of the distress of all creatures. 1.43.
Approaching the vicinity of each other's two ears to speak of Rāhu’s deeds,
they held conch-shells in their hands like the sun and the moon, as if they had found no opportunity [to speak] before.
Restrained by the circle of chamberlains at the command of the general stationed at the gate,
the gods remained in the sky and praised him with words faltering from joy.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Person, who stands even beyond the path of words and thoughts;
salutations to You who, by the power of compassion, have assumed a physical form in order to protect us once more from our towering delusions.
This entire universe is purified by the Bhāgīrathī, who has emerged from the lotus-feet of You;
what wise person is capable of measuring the purity of a person who contemplates You? (1.47)

O Lord of the three worlds, you possess infinite power and are free from transformation; these three powers of yours bring about the creation, preservation, and destruction of all things, both stationary and moving. (1.48)
O Supreme Mother, who by a mere sidelong glance leads the three worlds to the further shore of the ocean of existence—
salutation to you even once is indeed the fruit of actions corresponding to the effort expended.
You are light; you are the waters; you are the vast earth; you are the sky; you are the charioteer of Vaiśvānara;
you are the multitude of living beings; you are the Supreme; you are the Self—O Lord of the Universe, what indeed could there be that does not exist within You? (1.50)

We shall serve you, who possess the color of a fresh cloud, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, who are clad in yellow garments, and who wear a necklace and a crown; for what seeker of happiness would desire anything other than union with you? 1.51
O Lord of all, even the foremost Veda is not able to describe you in your entirety;
yet here you are, directly perceived once more—oh, our merits have been won in no small measure!
Regarding all the steps that captivate the minds of the ignorant as mere blades of grass, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
the great ones, whose wealth is dispassion, desire Your supreme abode which is free from rebirth.
Thus praised by the host of gods, the Lord— the storehouse of compassion and the night of destruction for the dānavas—
the sole protector of the world, rose and sat upon his serpent-couch, which was bent down by his weight.
On all sides, he gracefully warded off with his lotus-like hands the clamor arising from the golden bracelets of the playful celestial damsels of Vaikuṇṭha as they waved their chowries.
Having favored all the gods without exception, beginning with the lotus-seated Brahmā, with her gracious glance,
she spoke these words, making the ocean of milk swell with the floods of light from her teeth.
"Equipped with a strung bow, carrying a quiver, clad in armor, and holding a single arrow in his hand—this assembly of yours clearly forebodes fear from enemies to me. (1.57)
Enough with delay, O dwellers of heaven; let it be reported today: from what source does your fear arise?
This hand of mine, eager to slay the wicked, cannot tolerate Sudarśana obstructing its path.
Having bowed their heads many times to the Supreme Person who had spoken thus, those gods,
filled with the utmost joy, began to state their entire purpose.
Having restrained all those gods who were desirous of speaking with his hand,
the commander-in-chief summoned the Lotus-Seated One standing before him with a glance that was gracefully directed.
Then the Lotus-born One, having arrived, was taken by him [Brahmā] by the hand and led into the presence of the Lord;
having performed his salutation, he, being appointed to speak, made his representation in humble attire.
Although we have been granted prosperity by you, through excessive delusion we have taken pride in it;
now, seeking refuge in you once again in our distress, alas, we become the foremost among the shameless. (1.62)
Did you, bearing that exceedingly heavy burden of compassion, not act for the sake of us—those whose very birthplace is ingratitude—who are like a boat upon the shoreless ocean of suffering? (1.63)
Did you not, in former times, stretch out your hand before the Dānava Bali, even while avoiding the loathing that comes from accepting gifts censurable in the eyes of the wise? (1.64)

Did you not assume the nature of a human or an animal by casting off this divine form, in order to protect the entire world which was being overwhelmed by the king of the Daityas named Hiraṇya? (1.65)

By your diligent subduing of the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who had overwhelmed both gods and demons with his own prowess, did you not experience various states of being while becoming the son of King Daśaratha? (1.66)
Having sought refuge in you, our protector, in this very manner on many occasions—even now—we have come to you for shelter;
for indeed, it is the rain-cloud alone that repeatedly brings relief from the heat to the cātaka birds. (1.67)
Although you know all things, as if not knowing, O Lord, you inquire of us regarding the cause of our fear;
for this too is generally a method employed by masters toward those who have sought their favor.
O Blessed One, through fierce austerities the Danujas have attained the state of being unslayable by the gods;
having conquered both the netherworld and the earth out of pride, they now intend to conquer heaven.

The hand of Śakra is never empty of the thunderbolt, nor is his chest ever parted from his jeweled armor; and the lordly elephant does not remain unattached to him as he stands apprehensive of the approach of the Daityas. (1.70)

Desiring to seize the staff from Yama, the noose from Varuṇa, the mace from Kubera, and the thunderbolt from Indra, Kaṃsa—his hopes conquered by the prowess of his own arms—dispatches messengers. (1.71)
Having utterly defeated the host of gods in battle by his incomparable valor, the hero,
the lord of the Bhojas, now sports with his harem at the foot of the celestial trees.
With the tops of its ramparts occupied by archers, with all its foremost warriors busily engaged in guarding the gates,
and with cowards intimidated by great heroes, the city of the gods does not know how to stand still.
While this entire world, crying out "Alas!
Alas! in its helplessness, is being excessively tormented, no one other than you in the three worlds is able to bring about the destruction of Naraka.
Likewise, other Daityas, numbering more than a thousand, led by Pralambakeśin,
surrounded him, rending the sky in battles with their own lion-roars that were like thunderclaps.
O Mukunda, there are six sons of the Daitya named Hiraṇya who dwell in the depths of Pātāla;
by them, those misdeeds are committed against us which cannot even be described.
This earth is unable to bear the burden of those whose forms resemble great mountains;
therefore, placing us at her head, she has come into your presence to report her own distress. (1.77)
Having heard this petition of ours and declaring, "The Lord is the authority," Brahmā ceased his speech after performing a prostration; and that God also spoke with profound gravity.
Enough of this despondency, O dwellers of heaven; consider that which you desire is already within your grasp.
For this alone is my sole vow: the protection of those who have come for refuge.
"The two wives of Vasudeva and the wife of Nanda seek me, the son rich in virtues;
with two portions [of myself], I shall make all three of them, their limbs emaciated by vows, mothers of sons."
And this, my supreme power named Māyā, the mother of the three worlds, though herself devoid of birth and destruction, shall take birth, desiring to perform certain tasks for you. (1.81)

Therefore, go to heaven, free from distress; you should not fear any loss of time. I swear to you by this Śārṅga bow and by my arrows that I shall immediately remove the thorn of grief from your minds.
Having thus consoled that world of the immortals, the lotus-navelled god, who resembled a fresh cloud, suddenly vanished; and he,
having performed his salutation, praised his words.
With his mind overwhelmed by joy, he attained his own station.
Thus ends the first canto in the poem *Kṛṣṇavilāsa* composed by Sukumāra. || 1 ||
The Second Canto:
Now one day, Kaṃsa, accompanied by Vasudeva, went out in his chariot to visit his sister as she was performing her vows perfectly for the sake of obtaining sons in the outer grove.
There, with her slender body made to blossom by quivering luster and somehow bearing the clusters of her breasts,
he recognized her after a long time as a *ṣaṭpadinī* creeper hidden amidst other vines because of her locks of hair.

When her observance was concluded, that lady of graceful limbs paid homage to him, the eldest; and he, having favored the virtuous woman with a blessing, the Lord of the Bhojas spoke these words: 2.03. When her observance was concluded, that lady of graceful limbs paid homage to him, the eldest; and he, having favored the virtuous woman with a blessing, the Lord of the Bhojas spoke these words:
"You are still but a young girl; you shall give birth to many sons—why then these ascetic mortifications?
Behold now, at the time when the new shoots appear, does the mango creeper yield fruit? (2.4)
"You are emaciated; by all means, desist from these efforts for the sake of mental delights and enjoy pleasures.
O lady of supple limbs, how could your limbs, which are like lotus stalks, endure such suffering?"
Having spoken thus to her and, with her consent, having helped her mount the chariot together with her husband, he,
desiring to depart for his city, heard a voice in the sky that was like a hundred torrents.
"Staying near you, she will give birth to a son who is like the fire;
fanned by the winds, he shall be irresistible and will reduce you to ashes, O Kaṃsa."
Having heard those truthful words, Kaṃsa became exceedingly difficult to look upon due to the onset of rage;
abandoning all compassion, with sword in hand, he himself prepared to slay his own sister.
To him who was intensely engaged in a cruel deed, his lower lip quivering with fierce anger,
the wise Ānakadundubhi spoke words consistent with reason as he sought to appease him.
"Enough of this attempt at killing; O King, you must exercise reflection.
Has not the wise saying been heard by you—that misfortunes come upon those who lack discernment? (2.10)

O Lord of the Earth, how can your sword—having struck terror into Indra and the other gods in battles by making them turn their backs out of shame—now proceed toward this sin of killing a woman? (2.11)
What is the use of this life of yours, which would be preserved only by a simultaneous slaughter?
For those who have acquired even a name through some virtue, infamy is weightier than their own destruction. (2.12)
May there be no new stain upon this moon of your fame—which is ever increasing for one who seeks refuge and which delights the worlds day and night—due to the slaughter of your sister. (2.13)
"By the killing of his sister-in-law, infamy would befall him; therefore, even his friends would abandon him out of fear.
Thinking thus, those gods, conquered by his arms, surely employed this great stratagem. (2.14)
In time you shall see that which I have said; let there be no doubt in you regarding this matter.
Nevertheless, if your mind still hesitates, then listen to another way. (2.15)
"I shall deliver all my offspring, as they are born, into your power;
having considered their transgression or their merit, you may act toward them according to their condition. (2.16)
"What is the use of his own dullness of intellect, what is the use of that beautiful woman's good fortune,
or what is the use of the power of destiny?"— in this manner he accepted her words.
His terrible deed checked by the power of Vasudeva’s counsel, the sword-serpent, having turned back from its intent to kill,
entered the cave-treasury of the mountain.
"Could that bodiless voice have been true? Is this word of Vasudeva indeed the truth?
Reflecting thus, he reached the city, which was rich with jeweled archways and its banners raised high.
Placing his joined palms upon the crowns of the kings while they gazed at him,
he returned to his own palace, filled with dejection that remained fixed upon his face and inspiring fear.
Suspecting them, he placed those two in secret somewhere within his palace near his residence;
then, having subdued the entire world through his prowess, he enjoyed pleasures just as before. (2.21)
Then Māyā, the illusory power of Hari, brought about those sons of Hiraṇya who had entered the womb of Devakī;
the Lord of Bhoja, arriving in haste out of fear, killed them one by one as soon as they were born.

That portion of the Supreme Person which entered the womb of Devakī for the sake of the world’s prosperity—having drawn it away from her, the illusory power of the Enemy of Mura placed it within the womb of Rohiṇī. (2.23)
She shone with her son, concealed within the womb and pale as a saptacchada flower,
like the quarters of the sky belonging to the conqueror of Vṛtra when the moon is hidden by clouds.
Then, from her eyes which were full of joy, she gave birth to a son who was like the autumnal moon;
by his rising, the powerful kings immediately became as agitated as the oceans.
Having performed this task commanded by her husband, the noble lady, desiring to accomplish the remainder of the work of the gods,
she who is the progenitor of all worlds, mobile and immobile, took her leave of Yaśodā, the mother of her birth.

Then the Lord, the very birthplace of compassion, desiring the increase of his subjects, reached that Devakī—who was to be attained by the virtuous as the cause for destroying rebirth—for the sake of his own incarnation. (2.27)
Devakī, her slender waist marked by the weight of her breasts and her body-frame bent low,
bore within her womb the abode of the world, which was supported by the merit accumulated by the three worlds.
Vanishing from sight while purifying the earth with her own incarnation,
Devakī and the daughter of the sage both became mutual objects of comparison for the lotus-eyed one.
For Mukunda, the entire universe was not sufficient as a dwelling; yet, while residing within the womb, he rejoiced.
Indeed, for a man of great stature, suffering that arises from the service of others leads only to happiness.

The slender body of her, who was situated within the belly of Viṣṇu, possessed the hue of a madhūka flower— golden in color— as if by the radiance of the conch and the hand of Viṣṇu flashing forth from outside.
The slender woman did not wear a necklace upon her breasts, nor did she cast off the anklets from her feet;
she did not place the jewel upon her head for fear of its weight. That very state of being unadorned alone graced her.
She cast sidelong glances with effort, spoke softly, and laughed in secret;
she walked slowly with her friends holding her hand, and sighed deeply for that very long.
Along with the joy of the nectar-eaters, along with the merit of the earth, and along with the fear of the lord of the Bhojas, the divine Mukunda grew within the womb. (2.34)
Having manifested its splendor through the offerings of fruit brought upon the heads of the forest trees,
the rainy season arrived as if to behold Devakī, who had reached the time of childbirth.
Then, like fragments of the ocean scattered aloft by the city-wind,
the clouds shone in the sky, encircled by creepers of lightning and coral.
During the days when darkness born from masses of clouds stood before them, making them difficult to perceive,
there was no obstacle for the women going to meet their lovers except for the flash of lightning.
With its whistling, fierce wind issuing from within the bellows of the clouds,
the rainy season fanned the fire of love in the hearts of those separated from their lovers.

From the spring season, whose arrival was radiant and who was esteemed by Smara— the lord of the three worlds— as being no different from his own life, the birth [of the women] removed every trace of inferiority.
As if forcibly seized by the branches of reeds, all the rivers, having ascended to great heights as if intoxicated,
rushed forward with speed, laughing with their formidable foam.
Following the swarms of bees captivated by its noble fragrance, the breeze from the *ketaka* flower brought about a disturbance of the mind even in the God of Love.
To counteract the internal dullness arising from excessive drinking of water,
the clouds drank the rays of the sun, the friend of the lotus, under the pretext of contempt.
The fresh water, shining like the fruit of the date palm, gleamed in the forest pools;
it had been released by the masses of clouds after they had drunk it, like the mass of rays emitted by the sun.
Seeing their friend, whose feet had once been placed upon the heads of kings, now with his majesty shattered,
the bees in the sky cried out as if to die within a lotus submerged in water.
Having served him with sweet words and attained their desired object, the swans departed immediately at the time of his misfortune; for such indeed is the nature of those who dwell in the waters.

The forest regions, with their crops fully grown, densely filled with fruits, roots, and vegetables, and abounding in sweet, fresh water, bestowed supreme contentment upon the hearts of the common folk dwelling in the hamlets. (2.46)
The row of blossoms of the mountain jasmine, opening wide, shone forth most brilliantly,
like a garland of stars that had left the sky and descended to the earth out of fear of being crushed by the clouds.
In that season of boundless chill, where darkness was created by clouds pouring down torrents of rain, the sun remained unperceived anywhere; even by day, it dwelt as if within the fire.
When such a season had arrived— in the month of Nabhasya, during the middle watch of the night,
and while the assembly of planets was proclaiming auspiciousness— Devakī became ready for childbirth.
When the rainy season clouds had begun to dispel the heat of the world outside, the Goddess, as if out of compassion, brought forth the dark rain-cloud within him to quench his inner torment. (2.50)
The quarters of the sky became serene along with the rivers, and the ocean rejoiced together with the world;
and as Mukunda was born, the gods immediately released a rain of flowers out of fear.
As if proclaiming the increase of his fortune with the heart-delighting humming of the bees, the wind moved about, repeatedly seizing the garments of flowers from the trees. (2.52)
The sound of auspicious musical instruments resounded, mingled with the clear blast of conchs and the high-pitched strains of song, pervading the faces of all the quarters of the sky. (2.53)

Casting aside shame, violating discipline, suppressing moral conduct, and swiftly shattering fear, a joy that was indistinguishable from intoxication surged among embodied beings, born again and again from their unswerving births. (2.54)
Raising his hand high toward Āṣāḍhin, the world of the Brahman-sages, with their upper garments falling away,
danced with their feet moving in confusion, being laughed at by the celestial beauties.
As they were intent on sprinkling one another with floods of saffron water poured from their horns, an indescribable clamor born of joy arose among the nectar-eaters in heaven. (2.56)
Sons sprinkled their fathers, fathers their sons, teachers their disciples, and disciples their teachers;
wives their husbands, and husbands their wives, as they were intoxicated with joy, drenching one another with water. (2.57)
The lotus-born Brahmā sprinkled Indra; Indra sprinkled him who dwells in the lotus;
the two of them sprinkled all the gods without exception; and all the gods forcibly sprinkled those two.
They sprinkled one another with milk, shouted, leaped, and tossed their garments into the air;
they carried each other far upon their shoulders and became like those intoxicated by the joys of heaven.

Due to the joy arising from the appearance of the Lord of the Three Worlds, the minds of the celestial nymphs were so overwhelmed that the stumbling of the rhythm in their singing and dancing was not considered a fault. (2.60)
With eyes reddened by the splashing of water against their horns, their necklaces broken and their ear-ornaments fallen away,
the gods sported, conversing with words whose laughter was like the sound of rumbling clouds.
When Hari was born, desiring to remove the burden of the earth by the destruction of the demons, both the joy of the sage who delights in strife and the joy of the world arose together. (2.62)
Thus, while the multitude of embodied beings played unrestrainedly with minds agitated by great joy,
Kaṃsa and his servants, having fallen into a swoon called sleep, perceived nothing at all.

Beholding their son—dark-complexioned, four-armed, adorned with a noble necklace, wearing a crown, and his cheeks radiant with earrings—both the father and the mother became overwhelmed, immersed in bliss. (2.64)
Restraining his own overwhelming surge of joy, the son of Devakī spoke these words:
"Be gracious; I am exceedingly afraid of Kaṃsa, so withdraw this form."
Urged by him, he took up with both hands that [child] lying on the bed, who had assumed the state of an infant;
reclining upon those two hands of his, Padmanābha was exceedingly delighted.

What could possibly remain unaccomplished for him who, without any ascetic penances, formerly lay within the hollow of a banyan leaf while containing all the worlds within his belly— given that Murāri now rests upon the palms of his two hands?
At that midnight, when the circle of the quarters was oppressed by a mass of darkness as black as the *tāla* tree,
he took that lotus-eyed one and, departing immediately from his house, set out.
Having himself warded off the rainwater and illuminated the path with the luster of the jewels on his hoods,
Śeṣa whispered the means into the ear of Vasudeva and served Viṣṇu in many ways.

Having emerged from the city, he beheld the primordial Puruṣa carrying the flowing Yamunā; although her current was capable of eroding its banks, that daughter of Kalinda became as shallow as his own two ankles.
Having crossed it,
he joyfully entered the dwelling of the inhabitants of Vraja, led by Nanda, who had come to pay their annual tribute upon reaching the banks.
Having entered Nanda the cowherd’s dwelling, which was filled with bodies as if asleep,
he beheld Yaśodā, his wife according to dharma, who had given birth to a daughter and had fallen into a deep sleep.
Having laid him upon his own bed and taking the maiden with him, he proceeded on his way;
then he heard the clamor of the cowherd women, rooted in the joy of the birth of a son.
Carrying his daughter on his arm and his son in his mind, he traversed the road in an instant;
entering his wife’s house without hesitation and placing the child upon the bed, he remained there.
And that young woman, stealing the hearts of the world with a voice resembling the humming of bees, wept with her face slightly uncovered, which had the appearance of a blooming lotus. (2.75)
Hearing the sound of the infant, the guards, their sleep dispelled, rushed forward with speed;
having diligently awakened the Lord of the Earth, they announced to him that his sister had given birth.
Arriving there immediately and seeing the girl, he was overcome by indignation and devoid of discernment;
though forbidden by his sister, he, desiring her death, seized her two feet with both hands.
Having cast it far with his hand by force, that evil-minded one hurled it onto the surface of a rock;
though it had reached the earth, it remained suspended in the sky and blazed with a splendor like that of the progenitor of the worlds.
Then, with her hands radiant as lotuses, she who is the sole mother of the world, her multitude of weapons gently swaying, beheld him whose mental state was distraught and spoke these words: (2.79)

You grasped my feet even in anger; since I generally do not strike you for that reason, O wretch, a slayer of you has been born upon this earth. Reflect now on what is beneficial, for I am about to carry it out.
Having spoken thus to the king, she— like lightning illuminating the eyes of living beings with her radiance and causing them agitation—
ascended to the abode of the gods at great speed, her path through the clouds rent asunder, while her heroic deeds were being loudly sung by celestial maidens.
Hearing her words, which were harsh to the ear, he was deeply despondent within;
having consoled his sister, whose mind was pained by the misfortune of her son,
he then reached his own palace on foot and conducted himself there with great difficulty.
Kaṃsa, his heart agitated by anxiety, remained awake throughout the three watches of the night.
Thus ends the second canto in the poem *Kṛṣṇavilāsa* composed by Sukumāra. || 2 ||
The third canto:
In the morning, King Bhoja, having summoned all his ministers led by Pralamba,
spoke with humility to them as they sat in the places assigned by his gracefully darting glances.

Having doubted the words of Vasudeva out of delusion, I have—by that cruel man who has made the speech of a ghost his authority—slain my daughter and my sister; therefore, both my heart and my reputation are now turbid.
Furthermore, when my daughter, who possessed the luster of refined gold, was born, I desired to kill her at night because my life had reached its end;
but she, brandishing weapons and manifesting a divine form, leaped up and stood swiftly in the sky.
Restraining her indignation at the thought "he is my maternal uncle," that young girl became gracious and said to me:
"A great enemy has been born upon the earth; now is the time for you to consider what is appropriate."
When the goddess had departed for heaven after bidding me farewell, attended by throngs of celestial women,
I spent the night sleepless, reflecting upon my own wicked conduct.
In battles, the gods, led by Indra, were shattered by me and unable to stand their ground;
abandoning their horses, releasing their elephants, and casting aside their weapons, they flee in all directions.
Therefore, not even one among these who has come to my land is able to act in opposition to me;
for how could the pollen of a great tree ever succeed in facing the wind? (3.07)
What else could it be? Desiring to protect those in distress and showing his partiality toward the gods, I believe that very lotus-eyed one was born upon the earth to slay the asuras.
"We are all born from the lineage of Daityas, produced on earth for some specific purpose;
it was told to him by Nārada that he must arm himself to conquer us—this is indeed the matter."
Therefore, exert yourselves this very day, according to your strength, to destroy it while you are yet awake;
for once it has manifested as sprouts upon the tips of your fingernails, it will be beyond even the reach of the battle-axe.

"He who possesses affection for those who have sought his protection, who has a special attachment to Brahmins, and who bears a captivating form—that boy deserves to meet his death at my hands. (3.11)

Even the foremost Vedic revelation, which treats the power of all other people as mere straw, must be set aside—even those sacrifices performed for his pleasure must be prevented—if it merely extols his greatness alone. (3.12)
When this Garuda-bannered one has taken rest and all sacrifices have been forbidden,
and when all the gods are rendered weak, Amarāvatī will fall into our hands.

As he spoke thus, those men, proud of their prowess, made the quarters of the sky tremble with the sound of their boisterous laughter; while performing the lustration ceremony at his feet with the radiance of their crowns, they addressed him.
"O King, why do you worry? Enjoy the pleasures while we are alive; from where could an enemy come to you?
How could there be an eclipse of the sun by darkness while its rays are shining forth? (3.15)
O King, before long you shall behold the world where there is no wind, no bearer of oblations, no sun or moon, no wielder of the thunderbolt, and no Acyuta, Īśāna, or Pitāmaha. (3.16)
Having honored those who had spoken thus with appropriate offerings, he assigned them their respective duties;
and he released Devakī and Ānakadundubhi from their confinement.

A poor man does not rejoice so much upon finding a treasure, nor a cripple so much upon regaining his mobility, nor a blind man so much upon recovering his sight, as Nanda rejoiced at having obtained a son. (3.18)
When the sun had reached the western mountain and the quarters of the sky were shrouded in darkness,
Vasudeva approached Nandagopa, the inhabitant of the Yamunā bank, and spoke to him.
O Nandagopa, I believe that the austerity accumulated by you over a thousand births has now borne fruit, since this treasure of a son has appeared for you to discharge your final debt. (3.20)
"Here, near the city, a *kṛtyā* named Pūtanā, who delights in killing infants, plays;
therefore, this son of yours, who brings joy to the eyes, must be protected by you here day and night. (3.21)
Or rather, why do you remain here, having abandoned your own place in the vicinity of the city? The wise do not dwell in the presence of either a serpent or a king who is a companion of the wind.

Behold Vraja-Gokula, filled with people who are agitated and overjoyed at your arrival; it is adorned with festoons, full water-pots set down at the entrances, shimmering archways, and brightly burning lamps. (3.23)
I too have a child, the son of Rohiṇī, who is growing up in your territory;
he must be carefully observed and protected, for between us there is only a difference of physical form.
When he who was accompanied by Devakī had thus departed, Kaṃsa, filled with terror, somehow passed the remainder of the night;
then, as the sun ascended the peak of the mountain of sunrise, he set out toward his own dwelling.
Making the forest interiors resound with the noise of hundreds of carts, which caused circles of deer to start in alarm,
he then reached the joyful Gokula, where in every direction the rows of banners were shaken by the wind.
Having returned to his own dwelling, Nanda the cowherd, filled with joy, performs no work at all,
gazing day and night at the face of his son, whose eyes are as beautiful as the petals of a fresh lotus.
Delighting the hearts of the inhabitants of Vraja with his childhood, which was sweet with an innocent charm,
Keśava wandered about in Gokula, no longer even thinking of the ocean of milk.
Madhusūdana, desiring to drink, brought his face with both hands to the big toe of his foot;
then, as it were, the river of the gods flowed away under the guise of the radiance from the pearl-jewels of his toenails.
Like a second moon, bringing joy to the eyes,
that Padmanābha was led from house to house and from lap to lap by the women of Vraja with their hands.

Once, while lying beneath the cart, he whose eyes are like lotuses was gently raised by Yaśodā—who was preoccupied with her own chores—so that his lotus-like foot pointed upward as if in sport. (3.31)
Struck by the lotus-foot of the Slayer of Madhu, the cart instantly rose into the sky;
then, turning over, it fell upon the surface of the earth, filling the quarters of the horizon with its most intense roar.

Upon hearing the sound of the cart’s fall, which was like a clap of thunder, the cowherds headed by Nanda rushed there in haste out of fear, wondering "What is this?", their hair-braids falling loose as they ran.

With her lotus-like hands clinging to the jar-like breasts, her beautiful mass of hair loosened from its binding, Yaśodā ran after him immediately with her companions, accompanied by the tinkling of her jeweled anklets. (3.34)
Beholding her son, who was smiling and nowhere wounded, she was supremely delighted in heart;
yet, having learned of his prowess from the mouths of the inhabitants of Vraja living nearby, she was filled with amazement.
Thinking that his foot was merely dripping with blood, Yaśodā, having quickly approached, repeatedly wiped that naturally rosy foot with the hem of her garment. (3.36)
Having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead of the enemy of Madhu with dust born of cow dung,
Nanda the cowherd embraced him with his chest and meditated for a very long time upon his auspicious blessings.
Having seen the chariot of Madhusūdana shattered by the graceful play of his lifting his foot,
the sun then entered the interior of the ocean, fearing the destruction of his own chariot as well.
Smeared all around by the fresh glow of twilight, ruddy as a young sprout,
the quarters of the sky shone as if they had fallen into a fire due to their unbearable separation from the sun.
The ocean of the sky was long agitated by the immersion of the sun’s chariot; suddenly, it was covered with a mass of foam under the guise of shimmering, formidable stars.

When the sun had entered the netherworld, the boundless mass of darkness, perceiving its own destruction and trembling with fear, rose up swiftly as if from that very place and fell upon the surface of the earth. (3.41)

The earth, the atmosphere, the dwellings, the streets, the forests, the mountains, the rivers, and the oceans—the entire circle of the quarters was shrouded in darkness; nothing at all was perceived clearly by anyone. (3.42)

Then, as the third watch began and the people were somewhat quieted by sleep, Yaśodā, lulling her son—who was heavy with the joy of drinking milk—to sleep, sang softly: *atha prayāti prahare yaśodā jane ca kiñcinnibhṛte sanidre | putraṃ payaḥpānagurupramodaṃ prasvāpayantī kalamityagāyat ||* 3.43 ||

O son, you have a thousand cows belonging to you—possessing the luster of sacrificial pits, appearing like palmyra fruits, the color of the *tāpiñcha* flower, and the brilliance of the rising sun; they yield abundant milk and are as fresh as butter. (3-44)
Indeed, this mountain named Govardhana, whose ridges are filled with priyāla and date palms, and which is made beautiful by groves of plantains rich in fruit, stands as a son for your enjoyment.
Even though the forest of lotuses has gone to sleep, how is it that your lotus-eyes remain wide awake?
For those who possess familiarity with the sacred scriptures resort only to actions practiced by their own kind.
Curious to hear that sound and notorious for the destruction of infants' lives, Pūtanā—whose very body was like a torment to embodied beings—arrived through the sky. (3.47)
Descending from the sky, that night-stalker settled secretly in a certain place;
and when her lotus-eyed son was seen as if asleep, she too fell into slumber.
Placing Kṛṣṇa upon her lap, the merciless Pūtanā began to give him her breast—that breast by placing the face into whose opening an infant is deprived of life. (3.49)
Pressing with his two sprout-like hands the breast of Pūtanā as if it were the Pāñcajanya conch,
Madhu’s enemy then drew into himself the winds from within her mouth.
With her leaf-like tresses of hair scattered and the branches of her arms broken,
that night-stalker fell to the earth with a terrible cry, resembling a tree struck down by the wind.
Suddenly awakened from his deep sleep by that great roar of Pūtanā,
Nanda the cowherd, together with the host of cowherds, went to ascertain what had occurred.
Beholding the lotus-eyed one playing upon the body of that unconscious woman, they stood there,
their wonder fully awakened yet remaining free from any outward agitation.
They did not place their fingers upon their noses for even a moment. || 3-53 ||
Nanda, repeatedly wiping his eyes which were filled with tears, gazed upon his son who had slipped from the mouth of Death;
and he meditated upon him, desiring his ultimate prosperity.
He [perceives] that supreme reality with a concentrated heart.
Dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, a mass of dark hair, and a pure smile—while he was meditating in his mind, the Son indeed granted him His presence again and again. (3.55)
"It is not fitting for a heart that has transcended the attachment to sons to be occupied with the remembrance of Acyuta.
Thinking thus, he caused the twice-born to perform those rites which remove all sins without exception.

The Lord of Śrī pacified that terrible slaughter—which arose from the contemplation of Pūtanā’s conduct, which was heart-rending even for his father, and which caused universal desolation—by means of his pastimes that enchant all the worlds. (3.57)
Fixing his eyes, slightly rolling at the corners, upon his mother’s face with a pure smile,
Madhusūdana drank in her breast, supported by both his hands, as well as her very mind.
Bearing a face sweetened by drops of perspiration from the fatigue of walking about on his hands and knees,
Janārdana delighted the entire community of Gokula with his dust-covered body.
Once, while the son was wandering upon the ground, crawling on his hands and knees beneath the cows,
Yaśodā, intent on her household chores, bound him by force with a rope to a mortar.
For whatever kind of action a person performs, they invariably experience a corresponding fruit;
by that very act by which the Dānava Bali was bound in former times, he, though the lord of the world, then met with captivity.

While the Blessed Murāri, the bestower of liberation upon the entire world, was firmly bound to the mortar, a laugh arose in the minds of the circle of great sages, as their meditative absorption became loosened. (3.62)
"Sit down," she said with a smile, and having bound him with her glances, the lady with eyes like those of a cakora bird performed her duties;
meanwhile, the Lord of the Universe, turning the mortar around with indifference, departed from his own palace.
Having assumed the form of two *kakubha* trees by the immense power of Nārada’s curse,
the two sons of Kubera remained on the path as they were swiftly swept away by the current of the enemy of Kaiṭabha.
As he emerged through the path between two trees standing close together,
Dāmodara— the elephant among scented beasts— broke those two with his sideways movement, using the mortar as a goad.
Having attained their divine forms while remaining in the sky, both sons of the Giver of Wealth, freed from the curse,
bowed with devotion to the Ancient Person and, filled with joy, went into the presence of their father.
Nanda and the others, the residents of Gokula, immediately hearing that great roar born from its breaking,
approached those two *kakubha* trees, which were shattered and fallen.
There they beheld the lotus-eyed one, unharmed.
Having observed many misfortunes, Nanda gave ten thousand cows to the virtuous for the sake of the prosperity of his own son;
then, after consulting with his kinsmen, he quickly abandoned that place.
He departed for Vṛndāvana with countless wagons.
Having gone there, the lord of Gokula set foot upon a bank of the daughter of Kalinda that was pleasing to his heart,
and he took delight there, which was as beautiful as the station of Indra.
Beholding the playful antics of his son.
Indifferent to the churning of yogurt, to the boiling of butter, and to the milking of cows—
her eyes stolen by the joy of her son— Yaśodā passed days that felt like eons.
As Viṣṇu, intent on his rapid strides, pursued Nanda as if with a desire to seize him, his charming locks of hair, repeatedly turned back, shone forth by their very faces alone. (3.71)
In the midst of interruptions by those who had risen up, with utterances whose syllables and words were indistinct,
and with faltering attempts at embraces, he delighted the entire community of Gokula.
"Look at your maternal uncle! Thus addressed by Yaśodā in the nights, the lotus-eyed one summoned the moon with his graceful hand. (3.73)
Beholding his own reflection in the surface of the jeweled mirror held by his mother’s hand, the lotus-eyed one spoke out of curiosity: "Come, friend; what is here? (3.74)
Thinking as if out of compassion, "How shall this earth bear my weight?",
Mādhava, bearing the fear of falling, placed his footsteps very slowly.
At night, the divine Hari, resting on his mother’s lap,
listened with great reverence to her honeyed words,
while her thighs were gently struck by the sprout-like touch of her hands.
He fell asleep, his lotus-like eyes closed like buds.
Out of curiosity, watching Hari’s stumbling as he ran before his father, Yaśodā—her mind overcome with joy yet filled with bashfulness—neither remained still nor moved forward. (3.77)
Surrounded by a circle of curious friends who sounded hand-drums at his mouth, the Conqueror of Madhu,
assuming the state of a lordly elephant, took delight in his homes with graceful movements.
Then, as he continued to grow, Śauri took delight in curds and other such foods;
the women of Gokula began to bring him under their influence by offering those various items.
To the women of Vraja who addressed him with the request, "O Kṛṣṇa, perform a dance worth the price of fresh butter," he playfully raised his lotus-feet before them.
While the wielder of the Śārṅga bow stood thus for a moment, skillfully providing them with mental delight,
the Earth considered herself unfortunate merely from the loss of the touch of one of his feet.
Beholding his upturned foot, the Creator, his mind apprehensive of another stride, raised himself to perform the ritual washing, grasping his water-pot with the palm of his hand. (3.82)

Drinking that nectar of the dance from Kṛṣṇa with the cupped hands of their eyes, the women of Gokula became like figures in a painting, their minds rendered motionless by the intensity of their love.
Some, being overcome by the sight of him, were unable to give the fresh butter held in their hands;
others, having let it fall to the ground, did not even notice its absence from their lotus-like palms.
Thus Kṛṣṇa wandered incessantly among their houses begging for fresh butter— the very same [beggar] by whom,
it is said, the alms of Hara were turned back in the past by others who could not do so.
"Alas! This begging for curd is a superior means for removing the great sin of theft;
thinking thus, the slayer of Madhu surely fixed his mind upon the theft of butter. (3.86)
Having extinguished the lamp with the breath of his mouth while desiring to steal the fresh butter at night,
Kṛṣṇa was further discouraged when he was thwarted by the radiance of the gems adorning his waistband.
Pressing the earth with his forefoot and raising his body high with arms outstretched,
Trivikrama, reaching for the touch of the water-jar, became an object of ridicule.
Having somehow entered the inner chamber at night with controlled breathing and silent steps, Hari, the stealer of butter, turned back out of fear before his desire was fulfilled. (3.89)
As he set out at the thick of night, determined to carry off [the butter],
he moved very slowly for fear that the sound of his ornaments might be heard;
yet, because he entered the interior of the house where fresh butter was kept, [he was caught].
Alas, that night has already dawned upon the path!
Out of fear of meeting the cowherd girls and due to intense thirst, not knowing how to drink or even how to leave the cowherds' houses,
he went back and forth as far as the door of the vessel of curd.
The lotus-eyed one experienced only exhaustion while doing so.

Seeing his own reflection on the walls, he became apprehensive; having lost all desire for the fresh butter, he went out from the interior of the jeweled palace as if searching for something else entirely.
Desiring to carry off the dairy products within the inner apartments, he passed the days in devising means for that purpose;
and remaining ever vigilant, he spent the nights with captivating schemes for the abduction.
Even though he saw her moving close by him,
having resolved upon a suitable pretext to speak with her,
he placed a vessel of curd right near her.
Śauri [took] his own playful implements. || 3-94 ||
Carrying the butter he had seized, Acyuta, his lotus-eyes darting with fear, stood with downcast face scratching the ground with his foot; yet even so, he stole away the hearts of the cowherd women.
"I swear by my two parents that from this moment forth I shall no longer commit the theft of butter," Kṛṣṇa said, sighing deeply as he captivated the hearts of both his mother and father.
Though he was repeatedly entreated with respect by Yaśodā, saying, "Come, my son, to your home," Acyuta did not come, as if still wandering about, his face smeared with fresh butter.

"My fresh butter has been stolen from the churn; my ghee has been taken, and my curds have been carried off in the night"—hearing such words of women at dawn, he did not show any sign of agitation on his face.
Although entreated, the Blessed One whose navel is a lotus did not grant you— a protector of the lineage and of the world—
to me; rather, by the power of destiny, he gave you to one who is the sole thief of the world.
Yaśodā, feigning anger, spoke thus to her son.
Though repeatedly questioned by his mother through conciliation, persuasion, dissension, and even severe threats, Hari did not acknowledge his own theft.
"Having descended to the earth for the protection of the worlds,
Mukunda steals away everything from the dwellings of cowherds"—
hearing these mocking words of the gods in this manner, [he laughed].
The Blessed One, whose navel is like a lotus, laughed inwardly.
While the gopīs stood outside, having abandoned their homes out of curiosity to witness Kṛṣṇa’s playful combat,
he quickly returned home as if defeated by his friends.
Having fastened the door-panel, they took away the butter from within.
Stealing away everything from Gokula by means of countless methods worthy of veneration throughout the three worlds,
that son of Nanda took his delight there with the sons of the cowherds who were his own age.
Like the moon at the end of the rainy season, he is a cause of joy for all living beings. || 3-103 ||
Thus ends the third canto in the poem *Kṛṣṇavilāsa* composed by Sukumāra.
The fourth canto: Śauri, who had fixed his affection upon the son of Rohiṇī, who was the refuge of the virtuous and the dispeller of darkness,
grew day by day like the charming young moon, the lord of medicinal herbs.
Having abandoned his childhood state and incurred the reproach of being a thief, Hari,
I believe, became intent on rescuing the cows in order to wipe away that sin.
When his son was thus exerting himself, Nandagopa, having entreated all the sons of the cowherds,
commissioned them to protect him— the savior of even the three worlds.
Having had the rites for a safe journey performed by his mother at dawn, and having been embraced for a long time and bid farewell by his father,
the lord of the universe, filled with complete joy, set out for the forest together with Rāma.

Having eaten his morning meal, with hands still interlaced and carrying his staff, his horn resting upon his shoulder, he went from door to door in great haste, crying out loudly, "Let the cow be released! (4.5)
Hearing his sound, the cows— with ears pricked up, their tethering ropes cut, and filled with intense longing—
rushed out from their stalls in great agitation, even without looking for their own calves.
Moving like the king of elephants, the most eminent one, adorned with a circle of virtues, went ahead to the cow-pen,
filling it with his arrival for the sake of his circle of friends, together with the desired object of his parents.
At that very sound of Saṃjñāgava, which reached the path of their ears and touched the heavens,
the friends immediately departed from their homes, taking with them various kinds of household requisites.

With the great sound spreading in all directions, arising from the stamping of the cows' hooves and produced by the clashing of their horns, the cowherd settlement for a moment became composed entirely of that sound.
There Śauri sported in many ways with his friends who had gathered together, through long-distance running, leaping, and by forcefully releasing one another from their grasp.
The dust from the cow-dung, rising from the lotus-feet of the Ancient Person as He sported with His friends in supreme joy, purified the faces of all the directions. 4-11.
There, the great seers of majestic power, their true forms concealed and difficult to discern,
immersed themselves in the flood of pollen rising from his feet, which removes the torment of the fire of worldly existence.
While the people were watching with great delight as he performed enchanting sports,
Hari roused the sleeping cattle and goats in the cow-pen with a loud bleat.
While that enemy of the Daityas was departing for the forest out of a desire to tend the cattle,
the rays of the sun spread across the circle of the quarters as if wishing to announce the news to his beloved.
Shaking the flowers from the trees on the banks and drawing along circles of spray from the water,
the breeze from the Yamunā attended upon Kṛṣṇa as he walked, weary from his many pastimes.
As the Supreme Person was about to enter the forest with His lotus feet to protect Gokula,
the Sun-god rendered the woods fit for his entry with rays that dispelled the frost.

Having warded off his kinsmen— who, unable to abandon him out of love, stood with palms joined in supplication— Viṣṇu, placing Rāma at his head, entered the depths of the forest together with his circle of friends.
Beholding him as he entered the forest regions, exhausted by the heat of the sun,
the king of birds waited upon him in the sky with his outspread wings as a parasol.
"Do not go, Gaṅgā! Yamunā, where are you going?
Godāvarī, why do you run there?"—thus did Acyuta restrain the herd of cows that had strayed from the path, addressing each by its respective name.
He allowed the herd of cows to graze upon the forest lands where the shoots of very tender grass had sprouted, where the interior was shaded by shady trees, and where water was easily accessible.

The cows, with their long dewlaps swaying haughtily as they grazed and their tails curling, produced a *caṭat* sound from the clusters of grass snapping; this brought joy to the heart of the wielder of the discus (Kṛṣṇa).

There, as the cows, possessing the dark luster of emeralds, grazed freely upon the grass, Śauri attained a sense of fulfillment as if he himself had eaten; for the noble-minded find satisfaction by gratifying others.
While the cows, out of a desire to scratch themselves, held their necks high aloft,
the child Hari considered his own birth to be truly fruitless, as it was devoid of a thousand arms.
Entering the midst of bulls full of rut who were wandering about with fierce anger, raising clouds of dust, and clashing their bellowing horns, he brought them to peace.

There Śauri beheld with reverence the trees, which were bent down by flowers and fruit and were resting upon the earth, supporting themselves with the tips of their branch-hands; yet he was never satiated with looking at them. (4.25)

Seeing the low-lying areas where the roots were invisible due to extreme distance, where the stumbling of the water could only be inferred by its sound, and which were surrounded by circles of trees on high banks, he took exceeding delight. (4.26)

There he beheld creepers bent by the weight of their clusters of full, substantial blossoms, alluring with lips of tender shoots and rich with bees for their curls; seeing them, he remembered her who dwells upon the lotus.
Knowing the heart of Murāri to be longing to draw forth the daughter of the ocean, Saṅkarṣaṇa, the knower of all things, spoke these words with respect: (4.28)
O Śauri, this Govardhana, the upholder of the earth, with its cave-mouth resounding with a loud roar from the agitation of the internal wind, once again offers you a welcome.
Hearing the deep sound of the mountain streams at Govardhana, these peacocks of Kṛṣṇa dance with joy, as if born from the sight of you, their plumage fanned into circles.
Thinking, "These two feet are not capable of traversing this place," this herd of deer,
under the guise of clusters of rays from its own eyes, seems to cover the ground with blue lotuses.
Having scattered in all directions the honey dripping from the clusters of flowers of the forest trees,
the wind renders the earth, scorched by the rays of the sun, fit for you to traverse.

There is no fear within them, no flickering of their eyes, no concern for a blade of grass, nor even any restlessness in the young deer; enchanted by the beauty of Dāmodara, they stand motionless like carved wooden figures. (4.33)
Beholding that enchanting display shown by his elder brother,
the lover of Ramā took great delight as he tended the cows on the grassy lands.
Seeing there that Śauri of magnificent form, the Śabara women, their eyes having achieved their purpose,
approached with forest-grown offerings of fruit and spoke words graced by humility.
From here, you should go with this group of friends to a place only a stone’s throw away;
for the sons of the Kirātas will arrive here to protect these cows.
The Kirāta maidens will adorn you— the ornament of the three worlds— with pearls as bright as āmalaka fruits, released from within the frontal globes of elephants slain by hunters.
There is a certain maiden belonging to the lord of the Śabaras who is like a tutelary deity of our clans;
that king will by all means give her to you, along with great and priceless wedding gifts.
Observing with great respect in his heart the words thus spoken by the Śabara women, Kṛṣṇa, his mind overcome with compassion, spoke these words in a voice softened by bashfulness.
"O auspicious ones, having obtained the permission of my parents, I shall accomplish all that you desire. While I remain, Gokula remains safe; therefore, go, and do not be filled with despair."
When Mukunda, distressed by the failure of his desired [fruit], had consoled her, saying, "O Pulindī, go," those women,
having lost all desire for gathering fruits and other tasks, went slowly and dejectedly back to the hamlet itself.
Having dwelt within the bowers of creepers, having drunk the waters of the ponds,
and having tasted the fruits of the trees, Śauri made the forests blessed.
Then, when the sun had ascended to the middle of the sky with its unbearable mass of rays,
Halāyudha, observing the cowherd settlement distressed by the heat, spoke to the wielder of the discus (Rathāṅgapāṇi).
With herds of deer wandering among the slightly withered sprouts of creepers and young grass shoots,
and with the activities of people having ceased for the day, this middle portion of the day proceeds.
Behold the families of birds, with their young nestled between their wings;
with eyes heavy with sleep, they pass this harsh time within their nests. (4.45)
As if tormented by the harsh heat of the sun, the shadows have abandoned their outdoor excursions; they now dwell together with the travelers at the bases of the lovely trees.
This sun-girt one, scorching the earth with unbearable rays like a fierce sovereign, now assumes a contemptible state, as his subjects dread the spreading of calamity. (4.47)
Having traversed the vast wildernesses with speed, this lordly elephant, while proceeding to drink water from lotus ponds along the way,
sprinkles his beloved— who is distressed by the heat— with droplets from his trunk.
Scorched by the heat of the sun, the swans have left the waters that burn their claws;
now they wander slowly through the lotus pond, placing their feet upon the leaves.
Having with great difficulty released their own deceptive swords—their hidden intent to seize fish—these herons swiftly enter the groves on the riverbank due to the heat of the sun’s rays. (4.50)
Therefore come, let us go to this grove of trees; we shall bring the cattle here, who are distressed by the heat.
Having rested right here for just a moment, the cows may once again graze in the forest.
Having heard these words of Halāyudha, which were uttered in accordance with the occasion,
Kṛṣṇa said to Rāma, "As the noble one commands," and then entered the grove of trees.
Having approached a grove of trees that was like a garden, which had not yet received the entry of the sun's rays,
he, desiring to bring back the herd of cows, placed his flute to his mouth.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa standing there, gracefully turning his foot slightly, with his left eye raised in playful charm and his lips pale-red as he applied them to the flute, the world was filled with wonder.

There, the assembly of gods and siddhas beheld him alone— him whose eyes were as long as lotus petals, whose complexion was like the *tāpiñcha* flower, and whose crest was adorned with peacock feathers— and thereby attained the fruit of unblinking vision.
Standing in the triple-bend posture amidst the gaps of his flute, employing his sprout-like fingers,
he raised a loud sound capable of enchanting the three worlds.
Then the cows, their eyes closed in rising joy and their faces marked by freshly plucked blades of dūrvā grass, approached his presence and stood with motionless bodies and ears pricked alertly.
Natural enmity, attachment to offspring, thirst, hunger, and the god of love—these are not able to cause a transformation in animals who are intent on listening to the sound of that flute. (4.58)
In that enchanting forest region of the Discus-bearer, as the sound of the flute swelled forth,
all living beings, having ceased their activities, became as if painted in a picture.
As soon as they had entered the forest lotus ponds to give and take pieces of lotus stalks,
the ruddy goose and his mate stretched out their beaks and offered them to one another.
The circles of monkeys sat upon the branches of the forest trees, having abandoned their restlessness, with their faces resting upon their own knees and their gazes motionless.
Pressing the earth with both his feet and instantly straightening his upper body,
he stood there like a man-made lion, intent on attacking the lordly elephant.
The Siddhas, having risen in the vine-arbors to offer wine to their wives,
sat down with jeweled vessels raised by both hands, appearing as if they had entered into a painting.

Having properly partaken of the nectar of the songs of Acyuta fallen from the stalk of that lineage, the trees—though their bark was long worn out by old age—became as if young again, rich with fresh sprouts. (4.64)

Overpowered by the sound of the flute, the Vidyādharas dropped [their instruments] from their hands; surely the lutes fell before the Enemy of Madhu, as if thinking, "May our own gait also become such. (4.65)
Having thus filled the world of living beings with supreme bliss by the sound of his own flute, the Lord desisted; and all the immortals experienced a state as if they had just awakened from sleep.
When they perceived that your mind had returned, the lute slipped from their hands and fell;
then, overcome with shame, the Vidyādharas no longer entertained the desire to seize it.
A rain of flowers, released by the gods and siddhas, fell upon the head of the Supreme Person; it made the directions resound with the charming humming of bees and caused his bracelets to jingle.
When asked, "By whom was this heap of flowers, never seen before, rained down upon your head?
the Lord laughed and said to his companions, "How can you even possess knowledge of me? (4.69)
Having raised up the resting herd of cattle from the rays of the sun which had become bearable,
he began once more to drive them through the forests where the ground was dark with fresh grass.
Then, as the thousand-rayed sun was waning, the intense heat of the day subsided, just as the great pride of a wealthy man vanishes upon the destruction of his accumulated riches. (4.71)

As the sun, radiating rosy light, had deeply penetrated the western quarter, Rāma, observing the progress of the day, spoke respectfully to Dāmodara: 4.72. Behold, O Śauri, the delightful hour of day’s cessation has arrived: the movement of the gentle breeze becomes manifest, the heat is stilled, and all living beings find relief.
Carrying fuel, herbs, and roots upon their heads, calling out loudly to their own kind, the forest-dwellers, seeing that the day was drawing to a close, suddenly began to depart. (4.74)

Behold these birds, swift as thought, moving through the sky in hundreds upon hundreds with their garlands of feathers bound together; their restless wings are made resonant by the sound of "shāt," and they have made Indra’s tree their abode for the sake of prosperity.
Having rolled many times upon the dust of the earth and entered its nest,
the flock of sparrows gladdens its hungry offspring with morsels gathered by the hollow of their beaks.
Therefore come, O Śauri; let us go to our own place even before the heat has subsided.
This ravine, created by hunters, will later become difficult to traverse along its precipitous slopes.
Having heard these words of Rāma, Murāri said with great respect, "So be it," and set out together with his circle of friends, who filled the quarters with the fierce sound of their horns.
There Mukunda stood, joyfully waiting for the arrival of the cows at various spots, which were delayed far behind due to the weight of their udders as they hastened to join him on his journey.
Surrounded by the cowherd folk, Nanda stood on the road, and Yaśodā, surrounded by the cowherd women,
remained there with her eyes longing to behold the return of their son.
The sound of the conch blown by Dāmodara brought joy to the ears of those two;
then, as the cloud of dust spread through the sky, it rained nectar, as it were, upon their eyes.
Having approached those two princes whose limbs were grey with dust, Nanda embraced them firmly;
for a moment, he was unable to extricate himself from being submerged in an ocean of bliss.

Surrounded by cowherd heroes who leaped up and ran with weapons raised, filling the quarters of the sky with the roar of their shouts, he reached Vraja, where the sound of musical instruments was heard.
Having dismissed all his cowherd companions with flattering words,
Kṛṣṇa entered his home at the end of the day together with his friends, amidst the radiant glow of auspicious lamps.
Granted that during the day they had been led to Viṣṇu’s pleasure by the sound of the flute reaching their ears,
in the evening the cows returned his kindness with the sound of their milking.
Thus performing the protection of the cowherd settlement day after day, he passed his days in play as if they were but a moment; yet,
he was destined to lift up the entire burden of the earth.
There Śauri took his pleasure together with Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Thus ends the fourth canto in the poem *Kṛṣṇavilāsa* composed by Sukumāra.
